I want to like this game, and I really do in some areas. But it is definitely not at its full potential. And by that, I mean it's the weakest in the series.

Now, some context: I have, as you can see, over one hundred hours. I have played the game on infamous difficulty and completed it [spoiler]and all I got was a f*cking t-shirt and jeans[/spoiler] and thoroughly enjoyed playing some creative Arcade maps which I will get to in a bit.
Let's start the inevitable categories.

[h1]Control - How does the game feel?[/h1]
Ubisoft have actually improved dramatically on this front. The running, sliding, climbing and god damn ladders, all feel much more fluid and responsive. I've only played Far Cry 3 and 4 before this, so I'm going off of those for comparison. It was a bit weird going from more rigid animations to fluid animations, but I got used to it after a while. The ladders now allow you to directly jump onto them rather than having to start from either the top or bottom of it, which could allow some interesting custom maps.
Shooting is an interesting one. Instead of hitscan, the game moved to projectile bullets. This took some getting used to, and won't feel as satisfying as the instant sniper scope kills in the older games. At least, at first. After a while of getting used to it, it worked perfectly fine in its use case, though it sometimes makes guns feel a bit weak.
All of the stealthy stuff is still there, but it feels off. Throwing knives is more telegraphed, meaning you wont get those quick knife throw kills anymore. They're basically useless.
This is highlighted more below.

[h1]Gameplay - How does the game, well, play?[/h1]
Like your nan's apple crumble. It tastes good, but there's always a stray pube inside it or something that ruins the experience.
For instance, they've moved away from the "go to the next mission" approach and made the game more open ended. You can now kill the three perfectly reasonable Christians in any order you choose, as each one has a "liberation level" that gets added to every time you free a hostage, blow up a marked truck, complete a main mission, do a stunt, destroy a church, feed a grisly bear, burn druggies, make cows f*ck- wait hol up a sec
This is where it goes downhill. There is a lot of over-the-top action: going in loud, shooting dudes with machine guns, shooting them with bigger machine guns, explosions, rockets, bombs, HURK, and all the rest. There is so much emphases on loud gameplay now. Sure, stealth is still an option, but its either a rare mission requirement to not get spotted or a bonus at the end of an outpost. And that's it. You are not obligated to do stealth at all apart from those two single moments. The game's design supports more loud gameplay than stealth. 'Murica, I guess.
Speaking of,

[h1]Story - What's it all about?[/h1]
Tonight on National Lamp- wait i already made that joke
Basically, a doomsday cult has taken over Hope County, Montana and is causing a ruckus. You guys go in to arrest them like the good f*cking cops you are, and you end up p*ssing them off and making them commit literal genocide.
Whoopsie.
The story is honestly pretty bad, but it has so much potential. It tries to take itself seriously, but when you literally have a mission that beams someone into space to fight aliens, you just can't do that. The characters are all two-dimentional apart from Faith, who has some interesting story behind her if you go looking around for the various secret notes and phone logs in her territory. The other two sub villains are the token psychopath and a man who is experiencing a permanent 'nam flashback, and neither of them make too much sense.
The main villain is definitely not as good as the past two games, and his whole thing is about being right about the doomsday. That's it. No definition of insanity, no crab rangoon, just angry looks and snot physics.
Oh, and don't get me started on the ending. [spoiler]After an epic fight against a never-ending Joseph and touching up your friends who have been corrupted by bliss because you have the magic touch or something, Montana is nuked and everyone dies. Joseph was right. Whoopdie do.[/spoiler]
In short, the game is trying to make a point about how the world is getting closer to the edge, and it tries to foreshadow it with radio broadcasts throughout the game in what little time you're actually driving a car like a virgin and not just air dropping everywhere like a chad. It also takes stabs at current political conversations. Except it's trying to stab it with a wooden spoon.

[h1]Arcade - Those are custom maps, right?[/h1]
Yes. And they are awesome.
The game allows you to use not just its own assets, but DLC assets and assets from other games in other Ubisoft franchises. And on top of that, you don't need to own said games or DLC to experience those assets in maps. This is a big win for user content, and allows much more creative and flexible map-making. I have played some really cool ones and its why I come back to this game.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Only buy this game on sale if you want to get it, and I mean on a big sale. Humblebundle is a good place to check on for this game, as it is definitely, to me at least, not worth £40/$60.

Well, it's Far Cry. If you liked the previous game you're going to like this one too, unless you're tired of playing the same game over and over again. Some things have changed – exploration is rewarded better, for example – but it's nothing truly game-changing.

There's one big change which I sincerely hate. You get points for each accomplishment in the current area, whether it's a finished main mission, side mission or randomly generated activity like rescuing prisoners. When you earn enough points, the game will force you to fight the current area's boss – whether you want to or not. And after killing the boss many of the missions will not be available anymore, because you killed the boss. Basically, the devs created a content for you and then they won't let you play it. I have no idea how this could have been accepted.

[h1]Ultimate Hell Yeah Simulator[/h1]
Imagine you’re sitting there fishing in a peaceful lake, drinking a beer with some chill music in the background, and suddenly a bear just fucking mauls you. That’s this game, beauty mixed with chaos. A stunning landscape where you can hunt mystical LSD bears with helicopter missiles. Missions range from running over deer for roadkill meat to saving a sheriff from some MK-Ultra, other-dimensional brainwashing. It’s a proper redneck simulator with some insane villains, maybe not as iconic as Far Cry 3's Vaas, but still incredibly memorable. Especially Faith, whose dreamlike sequences give me IRL fever dreams.

However, this game has a huge amount of issues, it’s not a good game. In fact, it’s buggy, the AI is horrible, and stealth is borderline useless when the game suddenly decides you’ve been spotted. And why does a single-player game have microtransactions? If Ubisoft had spent as much time and money fixing the game instead of trying to turn it into a Garry’s Mod clone with recycled assets and DLCs so bad they make you want to uninstall, it could have been something great. Then there’s Arcade mode, somehow even worse, with an achievement for playing five Arcade Hero maps, which is hilarious when 95% of them just crash the game.

There are so many things wrong with Far Cry 5, but that’s the thing, it’s still really fun. And isn’t that what Far Cry is supposed to be? Ultimately, it comes down to what you want. If you’re looking for great storytelling, go play Far Cry 3. But if you just want to lose yourself in a beautifully broken sandbox of explosions, cultists, and wildlife that actively hates you, this is exactly what you need.

The short version: The game is enjoyable, fun to play with a friend, and might do well in the future due to the addition of Far Cry Arcade. It shows promise and I think it's a step in the right direction for Ubisoft. I haven't played for long enough to determine if the single player story mode gets stale. And, even though the AI might be considered sub-par, to me, the positives outweigh the negatives and I'd say it was even worth the full $60 I spent on it. I might very well purchase the season pass at a later date to see just how the game expands. So, yes, you should buy it, in my opinion.

Now, here's the long version...

Far Cry 5 is probably my favorite in the series, even having played the third game. The game itself looks, feels, and plays wonderfully. The PC version is well-optimized and I never ran into any problems with crashes, configurations, or just feeling like I'd rather play it with a controller. Combat is fluid, there's very few tedious quests in the game, and, overall, it feels like a new Far Cry while feeling very familiar at the same time. The setting encourages exploration and discovering secrets. Upgrading your character is interesting and, as I came to find out, entirely optional, since I didn't really give myself many serious perks until the very end of the game. Customization is a little lackluster but I'm not bothered by it whatsoever. The series has never given you the ability to create your own character in the past so I'm open and welcoming to it. And, while the game isn't entirely bug or glitch free, I'm certain that Ubisoft will patch the small issues that players like myself have experienced.

The only two real grievances I had with the game were ones I came to terms with after playing it for long enough. One is the AI. It's still far from perfect. In fact, it seems to have made no improvements from Far Cry 3. It's something you get used to, though. It's even fun, on occasion, to test the AI and see what you can get away with. It doesn't really take away from the game but I do wish it had been better. The other and more surprising concern is the fact that you can use real money to purchase in-game currency used to customize your character's appearance, for example. This sounded like an overwhelming negative, at first, having microtransactions in a Far Cry game. While you can find this currency through playing, I've only found a very small amount after exploring for twenty hours or so. However, I soon came to realize it was nothing to be worried about. Every unlockable can be given to you simply by progressing through the game. While you can instantly pay for the look you want your character to have right away, I wouldn't even recommend doing so. Not just for the obvious reason but because it gives you something to work towards instead of having it right at the start. Far Cry 5 is a fun game to progress in. Plain and simple.

The primary reason why I'm seeing this game get such bad reviews is due to the game's story. Many people hate the story, for whatever reason. In fact, a lot of reviewers say they hate the whole game because they don't entirely understand it. They think it should have some message to say about the state of America or religion as a whole or violence or any other subject that plays a large roll in Far Cry 5. I don't think it's about that, though. The game is different and interesting. It doesn't provide you with some takeaway message because it doesn't need to or even want to. It just wants to tell a story. A fictional story that reflects reality but never crosses the line. And I'm completely and totally in favor of that. I love how the game doesn't bring up modern politics or world issues to any massive extent. It's telling the story it wants to tell. It doesn't care what you believe or tell you how to think about something. It just wants you to enjoy the experience.

The only true negative thing I have to say about the story is that it sometimes interrupt gameplay. Your character might be taken hostage or captured at an inconvenient time. Regarding the story itself, though, again, I have nothing bad to say. It worked for me. I still had just as much fun with the game as I probably would have if it had been any different.

If you're one of the very few who read the long version of this, I hope you're no longer on the fence about whether or not this game is worth your time. Anything bad that can be said about it is overshadowed by the things it does well. If you're reading a review and it only brings up one or two negative facts about the game, make sure you take all of the positives into consideration before coming to a decision.

Again, short version: It's a pretty good game. You should get it.

While I'm a fan of the Far Cry series, the main reason I picked this one up was for the co-op story, something I wish they had done right in Far Cry 4. And something I'm still left wishing they did right. The game as a whole is fine, the world is beautiful and feels lived in, and the weapons are interesting and varied. Verdict:

This is, without exaggeration, one of the finest video games that has ever had the distinguished privilege of occupying my drive. The main story is thoroughly captivating, whilst the Arcade mode is an inexhaustible fountain of amusement. Together, they form a concoction so delightfully engaging that setting the game aside becomes an act of immense personal sacrifice. Acquiring the complete edition, accompanied by all the downloadable expansions, is an expenditure that shall yield returns far greater than many of life's allegedly sensible investments.

Story & Characters:

The narrative is, to my considerable delight, remarkably captivating. The true stars of this theatrical production are, of course, the alleged villains. Although, after a modest amount of contemplation, one is compelled to inquire whether they are villains at all. Each sibling possesses a distinct personality, an unmistakable aura, and governs their respective region with a flair that is impossible to ignore.

Curiously, I found myself possessing almost no enthusiasm for my supposed allies. Instead, I was eagerly anticipating my next audience with the Seed family. I wished not to engage them in combat, but rather to request a comfortable chair, a respectable cup of tea, and allow them to continue their delightfully unhinged philosophical discourse. They are simply fascinating individuals.

My allies, on the other hand, exhibit all the charisma of damp parchment. In fact, I refer specifically to that unfortunate gentleman whom one is compelled to dispatch after the villian starts serenading the room with Only You. Upon this rather abrupt and musically inclined encounter, I found myself not only startled by the circumstances, but also mildly perplexed as to his identity. The game had introduced him so many hours earlier that his existence had been thoroughly evicted from my memory, rendering the entire affair less a tragic moment and more an exercise in confused recollection.

Now we arrive at a matter of the utmost scholarly importance. Miss Faith. I would like the official record to reflect that I would enthusiastically SMASH Miss Faith on any day ending in the letter Y. Frankly, I comprehend with alarming clarity why so many individuals willingly surrendered themselves to Bliss. Had she invited me to partake, my resistance would have lasted approximately three and a half seconds before dissolving into botanical scented hallucinogenic enthusiasm. Whooweee!

Missions, Allies, Map & Arcade:

The missions presented herein constitute some of the finest interactive assignments I have had the pleasure of undertaking. Each one unfolds within an intriguing location, accompanied by thoughtful level design and an admirable capacity to consume one's attention for hours on end. A particular triumph is the collection of Prepper Stash missions, which are, in essence, delightful little puzzles that reward one's intellect with an almost embarrassingly generous quantity of valuable loot. I became so enamoured with these diversions that I felt an irresistible obligation to complete every single one. Such an obligation was, naturally, fulfilled.

The companion system is another rather splendid addition. One may recruit two artificial companions to accompany one's adventures, and I elected to travel with Jess and the distinguished canine gentleman known as Boomer. Their mutual appreciation for stealth aligned perfectly with my own refined tastes, for stealth is unquestionably the most elegant and rewarding manner in which this game ought to be experienced.

Jess deserves particular commendation. She frequently remarks upon nearby locations, recently encountered individuals, or the wildlife one has thoughtfully identified, lending the world an unexpectedly immersive quality. Her observations often feel natural and delightfully contextual. Regrettably, during extended journeys she occasionally begins vocalising thoughts of such bewildering triviality that one is left questioning whether prolonged exposure to Montana's fresh air has adversely affected her faculties. I have yet to use the remaining companions, although Hurk continues his proud tradition of possessing approximately the same quantity of intellectual substance as a decorative sack of fecal matter. Some traditions, it seems, transcend individual titles.

Whenever presented with the opportunity, I elected to proceed with the utmost stealth. Hunting cultists across the countryside is an activity of extraordinary satisfaction, particularly when one imposes delightfully unnecessary restrictions upon oneself. On one occasion I liberated an outpost armed solely with a pistol. On another, only a sniper rifle. Sometimes merely an assault rifle. Occasionally nothing more than a pistol and a collection of aggressively persuasive takedowns. None of this was required. Every bit of it was immensely entertaining.

The outposts themselves deserve abundant praise. Rather than presenting the same monotonous assortment of jungle encampments that Ubish!t appears to contractually obligated to provide, each location possesses its own identity, architecture, and tactical considerations. One may find oneself infiltrating farms, churches, lumber mills, marinas, airfields, or any number of equally fascinating locales. Every establishment is generously decorated with notes, answering machines, journals, and assorted fragments of environmental storytelling that reward those possessing the rare virtue of curiosity.

The transformation following liberation is equally gratifying. During cult occupation, each outpost is adorned with all manner of unsettling Bliss related paraphernalia and other deeply questionable interior decorating decisions. Once reclaimed, the Resistance promptly removes this decorative fecal matter and restores the premises to a far more civilised condition. The accompanying liberation cinematic remains one of the most satisfying little rewards in the entire game, shamelessly congratulating me for my heroics. I accepted these congratulations with the humility one would expect from a man who had just single handedly reclaimed an enemy stronghold.

Another decision worthy of enthusiastic applause concerns the world map. Rather than assaulting one's retinas with the customary avalanche of Ubish!t map icons before the tutorial has even concluded, Far Cry 5 has the decency to permit discovery. One uncovers locations through exploration, by acquiring maps, or through the positively revolutionary act of conversing with other human beings. Residents of liberated outposts happily point you towards interesting characters, side quests, and hidden locations, allowing progression to emerge naturally instead of resembling an administrative spreadsheet with firearms. A concept both novel and refreshing.

Finally, there is Arcade. Good heavens. The Solo Arcade maps are so absurdly magnificent that they elevate the entire package into another realm altogether. The craftsmanship displayed by many of these creations borders upon wizardry. I have already ventured through a respectable assortment of them, and each has been an absolute delight to explore. Some of these community creations are so visually exquisite that I found myself wondering whether the principal campaign had been quietly outsourcing its architecture to a less talented cousin. The Arcade alone adds a frankly indecent quantity of value to an already exceptional game.

Perfectly fine "fast food" gaming, Far Cry 5 is not trying to be the greatest at anything and it offers a decent (if ultimately unessential) time as a result. 

I'd recommend it on sale if you're just looking for a competent game to chew on for a few sessions, I got it 85% off and enjoyed my time but wouldn't have liked to pay more than the £7.49 it cost me.
